questions.stem: An 84 year old man with mild Alzheimer's disease lives with his wife and usually chats, dresses himself and recognises his family. Over 36 hours he has become muddled and distractible, and cannot recite the months backwards. He is lucid in the morning but agitated by evening. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute change over hours to days with fluctuating inattention, on top of dementia, is delirium. Alzheimer's progression is gradual.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: lucid in the morning but agitated by evening
steps.x: **Acute** onset, **inattention** and **fluctuation** on a background of dementia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Delirium superimposed on dementia.

elim: Gives low mood and slowing over weeks, not fluctuating inattention over hours.
Fluctuates, but develops over months with parkinsonism and hallucinations.
Alzheimer's progresses slowly over months to years, not over 36 hours.
Progresses stepwise over months, without acute inattention.

steps.x: **A. Delirium.** Delirium: acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition over hours to days.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman is 3 days after a hip fracture repair. Overnight she shouted, pulled out her cannula and tried to climb out of bed. Today she is sleepy, barely speaks and drifts off mid-sentence. Her 4AT score is 8. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which subtype of delirium is most likely?
questions.e: Alternating agitation and drowsiness is mixed delirium. Hyperactive or hypoactive delirium alone would show only one pattern.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Agitated** at night, **drowsy** by day: both patterns.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mixed delirium.

elim: An alcohol withdrawal state; there is no alcohol history.
Only part of the picture; she is also drowsy and withdrawn.
Only part of the picture; she was agitated overnight.
She has a positive 4AT and an acute post-operative change, so this is delirium.

steps.x: **D. Mixed delirium.** Subtypes: hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (drowsy, easily missed), mixed (both).

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is admitted with pneumonia. On day 2 he is restless, pacing the ward and trying to leave. He is disorientated in time and place and cannot follow a conversation. He is hitting out at staff who approach him. He was independent and orientated before admission. His temperature is 38.2°C.
questions.q: Which subtype of delirium is most likely?
questions.e: Agitation, restlessness and disorientation during an acute illness is hyperactive delirium.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
An **acute** change with **agitation and restlessness**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hyperactive delirium.

elim: Gives immobility and mutism, not restlessness.
Would be drowsy and quiet.
He has only shown agitation, not alternating drowsiness.
Has no acute inattention and disorientation caused by illness.

steps.x: **B. Hyperactive delirium.** Hyperactive delirium: agitation and restlessness.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man is 3 days into an admission for a fractured ankle. He has become agitated and disorientated, and says there are spiders on the wall. He is sweating and tremulous. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 162/96 mmHg and temperature 37.6°C. His GGT is 340 U/L (<55) and MCV 104 fL (80–100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his delirium?
questions.e: Agitation, visual hallucinations, tremor, sweating and tachycardia 3 days into admission with a high GGT and MCV is alcohol withdrawal delirium, which can also cause seizures.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Autonomic overactivity** and **hallucinations** on day 3, with markers of **heavy drinking**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcohol withdrawal.

elim: Would give dry skin, retention and dilated pupils rather than sweating and tremor.
Gives hypoxia and petechial rash 1 to 3 days after long-bone fracture.
Would give pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing.
Does not explain tremor, sweating and the markers of heavy drinking.

steps.x: **E. Withdrawal from alcohol.** Alcohol excess is a cause of delirium (and seizures).

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is 1 day after a laparotomy. She is on a morphine PCA. Nurses report she has become confused and very drowsy. Her respiratory rate is 9 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L oxygen, pulse rate 70 bpm and temperature 36.9°C. Her pupils are pinpoint. Her capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her delirium?
questions.e: Drowsy confusion with a slow respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils on a morphine PCA is opioid toxicity, a drug cause of delirium.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Slow breathing** and **pinpoint pupils** on **morphine**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Opioid toxicity.

elim: Would give agitation, sweating and tachycardia.
Her glucose is normal.
She is afebrile with a normal pulse.
No focal signs, and pinpoint pupils with slow breathing fit opioids.

steps.x: **C. Opioid toxicity.** Medications (opioids, anticholinergics) are common precipitants of delirium.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman has hyperactive delirium from a chest infection. She keeps getting out of bed at night and walking to the door, even though she uses a frame at home. She is on a general medical ward. Her BP is 118/68 mmHg lying and 102/60 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which complication is she at greatest immediate risk of?
questions.e: Delirium raises the risk of falls, especially with wandering at night, a walking frame and postural hypotension.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: getting out of bed at night
steps.x: Wandering, **unsteady** and **postural drop**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Falls.

elim: Not the main immediate risk from her behaviour.
More likely in hypoactive, immobile patients.
She is mobile, not bed-bound.
Not suggested here.

steps.x: **B. Falls.** Delirium complications: falls, longer hospital stay, increased mortality.

questions.stem: An 88 year old man has had delirium for 5 days due to a urinary infection. He is improving on antibiotics. His daughter asks how the delirium will affect his outcome compared with patients admitted with the same infection who do not become delirious.
questions.q: Which outcome is most strongly associated with delirium?
questions.e: Delirium is associated with increased mortality, more falls and a longer hospital stay.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
What does delirium **add** to the illness?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Increased mortality.

elim: Delirium increases falls.
Delirium is linked to later cognitive decline, not protection.
Delirium prolongs hospital stay.
Delirium often persists for days to weeks.

steps.x: **B. Raised risk of death.** Delirium: higher mortality, more falls, longer stay.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman with hay fever was started on chlorphenamine 4 days ago. She takes amlodipine, atorvastatin and levothyroxine, all for years. She is now confused and restless, has a very dry mouth and has not passed urine for 10 hours. Her bladder is palpable. Her pupils are dilated and her temperature is 37.3°C.
questions.q: Which medication is the most likely cause of her delirium?
questions.e: Chlorphenamine is an anticholinergic antihistamine; new confusion with dry mouth, dilated pupils and urinary retention shows central and peripheral anticholinergic effects.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**New** drug, then **dry mouth**, **retention** and **dilated pupils**: anticholinergic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chlorphenamine.

elim: Long-standing and not anticholinergic.
Long-standing and not anticholinergic.
Long-standing; would only cause problems if over-replaced.
She is not taking it, and it does not cause anticholinergic effects.

steps.x: **C. Chlorphenamine.** Anticholinergics (chlorphenamine, promethazine) cause delirium with dry mouth and retention.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman's son is worried she has dementia. She was well until 2 days ago, when she became muddled after a fall. She now loses track of conversations, cannot say the days of the week backwards and is better at some times than others. Her temperature is 37.9°C.
questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from dementia in her?
questions.e: Delirium is an acute disturbance (hours to days) mainly of attention, which fluctuates; dementia develops over months with preserved attention early on.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: better at some times than others
steps.x: The onset is **days**, and **attention** is what has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute onset with inattention.

elim: Occurs in both delirium and dementia.
Both are common in older people.
Occurs in both.
Occurs in both, and is common in dementia.

steps.x: **D. Sudden onset with impaired attention.** Delirium = acute + inattention + fluctuation; a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man is admitted with cellulitis. Nurses notice that during the morning ward round he answers questions sensibly, but each evening he becomes confused, cannot keep his attention on a task and tries to leave the ward. His 4AT score is 7 in the evening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of his symptoms?
o: Fluctuating confusion, worse at certain times of day
Sudden permanent confusion after one event
questions.e: Delirium causes fluctuating consciousness, characteristically worse at certain times of day such as the evening. Dementia progresses gradually.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Lucid** in the morning, **confused** in the evening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluctuating, worse at certain times.

elim: Delirium characteristically fluctuates.
Typical of dementia.
Typical of vascular dementia.
Suggests a stroke or brain injury.

steps.x: **B. Fluctuating confusion, worse at certain times of day.** Delirium fluctuates: worse at certain times of day.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has 1 day of new confusion and agitation. He has passed only dribbles of urine and keeps holding his lower abdomen. His temperature is 37.0°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. There is a dull, tender mass rising out of the pelvis. A bladder scan shows 1.3 L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his delirium?
questions.e: Acute urinary retention from his prostate is the cause; catheterisation treats both the retention and the delirium.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
A **1.3 L** bladder in a man with **BPH**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute urinary retention.

elim: Can cause retention and delirium, but the clear finding here is a 1.3 L bladder.
He is not on opioids.
No focal signs.
He is afebrile; the bladder scan explains the picture.

steps.x: **D. Urinary retention.** Treat the cause: catheterise urinary retention.

questions.stem: An 89 year old woman lives alone. During a heatwave she became confused and drowsy over 2 days. She has a dry tongue and reduced skin turgor. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Investigations show urea 18.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), creatinine 128 µmol/L (45–90) and sodium 149 mmol/L (135–145). Urine and chest X-ray are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her delirium?
questions.e: A heatwave, dry tongue, tachycardia and raised urea and sodium show dehydration, a minor insult that can tip an older person into delirium; treat with IV fluids.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Dry**, **tachycardic** with a **high urea and sodium**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dehydration.

elim: Does not explain the dry tongue and raised urea and sodium.
Her chest X-ray is normal.
No focal signs.
Her urine is normal.

steps.x: **A. Dehydration.** Find and treat the cause: IV fluids for dehydration.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman becomes acutely confused on the ward on day 3 of an admission for heart failure. Her attention fluctuates and she cannot name the months backwards. The F2 doctor asks which test will confirm that she has delirium.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Clinical assessment of attention and cognition
questions.e: Delirium is a clinical diagnosis, made from an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition, screened with the 4AT. Tests look for the cause.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
No blood test or scan diagnoses delirium itself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical assessment.

elim: Looks for structural causes but does not diagnose delirium.
Not used routinely to diagnose delirium.
Only if meningitis or encephalitis is suspected.
Looks for a cause, not the delirium itself.

steps.x: **A. Clinical assessment of attention and cognition.** Delirium is a clinical diagnosis; tests are for the underlying cause.

questions.stem: An 85 year old man has become muddled on the ward. Using the 4AT he is alert, gives his age but not the date or place, gets the months backwards wrong after 3, and his nurse reports an acute change over 24 hours. His total 4AT score is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: 4AT score
visual.label: Score 8
visual.caption: A 4AT of 4 or more suggests possible delirium.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of his score?
questions.e: A 4AT score of 4 or above suggests possible delirium, with or without underlying cognitive impairment. Scores of 1 to 3 suggest possible cognitive impairment.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
The 4AT threshold: **4 or above**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Possible delirium.

elim: A score of 4 or more suggests possible delirium.
The 4AT is a delirium screen; it does not confirm dementia.
An acute change and a score above 4 are not normal.
That is the meaning of a score of 1 to 3.

steps.x: **E. Possible delirium.** 4AT ≥4 = possible delirium (with or without cognitive impairment).

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide is brought in by his wife with 2 hours of confusion. He is sweaty and disorientated. He ate very little today because of a stomach bug. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. There are no focal neurological signs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Sudden confusion is an emergency needing an urgent search for the cause; in a sweaty patient on a sulfonylurea who has not eaten, check glucose first.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
**Sulfonylurea**, **not eating**, **sweaty**: hypoglycaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capillary blood glucose.

elim: A screening tool; the urgent priority is the cause.
No focal signs; first exclude a reversible metabolic cause at the bedside.
Not first-line without signs of meningitis.
Part of the infection screen, but glucose is the urgent test here.

steps.x: **B. Capillary blood glucose.** Delirium bloods include glucose; sudden confusion always needs an urgent cause search.

questions.stem: An 87 year old woman in a care home has 2 days of confusion and drowsiness. She has a new cough with green sputum. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the right base. Her urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
questions.e: Cough, sputum, fever and right basal crackles point to pneumonia as the cause of delirium, confirmed by chest X-ray.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.

clues: coarse crackles at the right base
steps.x: The **chest** is the likely source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chest X-ray.

elim: No focal signs or head injury.
No suggestion of constipation.
Not routine.
Her urine dipstick is negative and the chest is the source.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Delirium work-up: infection screen, bloods, chest X-ray, medication review, stool chart/DRE.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has had 3 days of fluctuating confusion. He has no fever, urinary symptoms, cough or constipation. FBC, U&Es, CRP, glucose, urine culture and chest X-ray are normal. In the last week his GP started oxybutynin, amitriptyline for neuropathic pain and codeine.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in identifying the cause?
questions.e: With a negative infection and blood screen, review medications: oxybutynin and amitriptyline are anticholinergic and codeine is an opiate, all causes of delirium.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
**Three new drugs**, two anticholinergic and one opiate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Medication review.

elim: No focal signs or head injury.
No features of CNS infection.
Not first-line; there is an obvious drug cause to look at.
Not relevant.

steps.x: **C. Medication review.** Once delirium is suspected, search for the cause including a medication review.

questions.stem: A 90 year old woman in a nursing home has 1 day of new agitation and confusion. Staff say she is going to the toilet more often and her urine smells offensive. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/70 mmHg. Her chest is clear. She has no new medications and normal bowels.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
questions.e: UTI is the single most common cause of delirium; frequency and offensive urine in an over-65 should be confirmed with urine culture, not dipstick alone.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.

clues: going to the toilet more often
steps.x: **Urinary** symptoms in a confused older woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urine culture.

elim: No focal signs or head injury.
Her bowels are normal.
Not routine.
For hepatic encephalopathy, which is not suggested.

steps.x: **D. Midstream urine culture.** Infection, especially UTI, is the commonest cause of delirium.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman has delirium from pneumonia and is on antibiotics. She is calm but keeps asking what day it is and where she is. She wears glasses and a hearing aid, which are in her bag. Her family live nearby. She is not a risk to herself or others.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate measure to add, in line with NICE delirium guidance?
o: Lorazepam at night to help sleep
Moving her to a different bay each night
Physical restraint to keep her in bed
Reorientation with a clock, calendar, her glasses and hearing aid
questions.e: First-line for all patients is non-drug care: one-to-one supervision and reorientation with clocks, calendars, aids, family, good lighting and hydration.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: not a risk to herself or others
steps.x: Calm, **disorientated**, sensory aids **unused**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reorientation measures.

elim: Sedation is not needed; she is calm.
Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium.
Changes of environment worsen delirium.
Not appropriate and increases harm.

steps.x: **E. Reorientation with a clock, calendar, her glasses and hearing aid.** First-line for all: supervision and reorientation, not drugs.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with delirium from a UTI is pulling at his cannula and shouting at the nurse, saying she is trying to poison him. He has no Parkinson's disease or dementia. He is on IV antibiotics. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. No one has yet tried to calm him.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of his agitation?
questions.e: If there is risk to self or others, first-line is verbal de-escalation: calm, non-confrontational reassurance and reorientation. Drugs come only if it fails.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: No one has yet tried to calm him
steps.x: A risk to himself, but **nothing has been tried** yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Verbal de-escalation.

elim: Rapid tranquillisation is a last resort.
Second-line if de-escalation fails.
Not first-line and increases harm.
They treat the cause.

steps.x: **E. Verbal de-escalation.** Risk to self/others: verbal de-escalation first, then drugs.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman with Lewy body dementia has delirium from a chest infection. Despite one-to-one nursing and verbal de-escalation, she is hitting staff and trying to climb over the bed rails. She is taking oral medicines. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
questions.e: In Lewy body dementia or Parkinson's, a benzodiazepine such as oral lorazepam is used if sedation is needed; antipsychotics are avoided because of anti-dopaminergic side effects.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: Despite one-to-one nursing and verbal de-escalation
steps.x: **Lewy body dementia**: never an antipsychotic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral lorazepam.

elim: Anticholinergic; would worsen delirium.
Antipsychotics are avoided in Lewy body dementia.
Antipsychotics can cause severe reactions in Lewy body dementia.
Anticholinergic; would worsen delirium.

steps.x: **D. Oral lorazepam.** Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia: lorazepam, never an antipsychotic.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with delirium from pneumonia is trying to hit staff. One-to-one care and verbal de-escalation have failed. He has no Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia. He is willing to take tablets. His ECG shows a normal QT interval. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
questions.e: If sedation is needed without Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia, low-dose haloperidol is second-line, using the least invasive route: oral before IM.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: no Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia
steps.x: De-escalation failed, **no Parkinson's/Lewy body**, **takes tablets**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low-dose oral haloperidol.

elim: Oral is tried first as it is less invasive, since he will take tablets.
Kept for rapid tranquillisation.
Anticholinergic; worsens delirium.
Benzodiazepines are for Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia, or rapid tranquillisation.

steps.x: **C. Low-dose oral haloperidol.** Second-line: low-dose haloperidol, oral first, then IM.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with hyperactive delirium has pulled out his central line and is swinging a drip stand at staff. Verbal de-escalation has failed, he refuses all oral medication and he is an immediate danger to himself and others. He has no Parkinson's disease. Security are present.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication for rapid tranquillisation?
questions.e: For rapid tranquillisation, IM lorazepam is used. Oral drugs are not possible when he refuses them.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: immediate danger to himself and others
steps.x: **Immediate danger**, **no oral route**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IM lorazepam.

elim: He refuses oral medication.
He refuses oral medication.
Anticholinergic and oral.
He refuses oral medication.

steps.x: **A. IM lorazepam.** Rapid tranquillisation: IM lorazepam.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman has 2 days of confusion, agitation and seeing people in her room. She has lower abdominal discomfort and urinary frequency. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg. Her eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73m². Urine culture grows E. coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her delirium?
questions.e: Delirium is managed by treating the underlying cause directly: antibiotics for her UTI. Sedation does not treat the cause.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
UTI-related delirium: **treat the infection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Nitrofurantoin.

elim: Not needed; the cause is clear.
Sedation does not treat the cause.
Can worsen delirium.
Harmful and not a treatment.

steps.x: **D. Nitrofurantoin.** Treat the cause: antibiotics for UTI.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man was admitted 6 days ago with a rib fracture and is on regular oral morphine. Over 2 days he has become confused and restless. He has not opened his bowels for 6 days. His abdomen is distended and DRE shows hard faeces in the rectum. His urine and chest X-ray are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Constipation and faecal impaction, common in older inpatients on opiates, are treated with laxatives (and an enema for impaction).

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: not opened his bowels for 6 days
steps.x: **Opiates** + **impacted faeces**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Laxatives and an enema.

elim: Does not treat the cause.
Will worsen constipation.
His urine is normal.
There is no retention.

steps.x: **C. Laxatives and an enema.** Constipation causes delirium in inpatients on opiates: treat with laxatives.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman has 4 days of new confusion, dry mouth and constipation. Her GP started oxybutynin for urge incontinence a week ago. Her infection screen, bloods and chest X-ray are normal. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and causes delirium through central cholinergic deficiency; review and stop causative drugs.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: infection screen, bloods and chest X-ray are normal
steps.x: A **new anticholinergic** with dry mouth and normal screen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop the oxybutynin.

elim: Not used to treat delirium.
Sedation does not treat the cause.
Will worsen her delirium.
There is no infection.

steps.x: **E. Stop oxybutynin.** Stop or review causative drugs: anticholinergics, opiates, anticonvulsants.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man develops delirium on day 2 of an admission with severe sepsis from pneumonia. His CT head and MRI brain are normal. After 10 days of antibiotics his confusion has fully resolved.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his delirium?
o: Systemic illness causing diffuse cerebral dysfunction
questions.e: Delirium is acute, diffuse cerebral dysfunction driven by a systemic insult such as infection, rather than primary structural brain disease; inflammatory cytokines cross the blood-brain barrier and disrupt neurons, so it resolves with treatment.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: CT head and MRI brain are normal
steps.x: **Normal imaging** and **full recovery** after treating a **systemic** illness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diffuse cerebral dysfunction from systemic illness.

elim: Imaging is normal and it resolved.
Would cause abnormal imaging and needs aciclovir.
Alzheimer's disease, which is gradual and does not resolve.
Imaging is normal.

steps.x: **E. Systemic illness causing diffuse cerebral dysfunction.** Delirium: systemic insult, not structural brain disease.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with hyperactive delirium from pneumonia is given low-dose oral haloperidol after verbal de-escalation fails. Within an hour her agitation settles. She has no Parkinson's disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which haloperidol helped?
questions.e: Delirium involves relative dopaminergic excess with cholinergic deficiency; haloperidol, a dopamine antagonist, settles agitation.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Haloperidol is a **dopamine antagonist**; delirium has **dopamine excess**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: D2 blockade.

elim: Anticholinergic action would worsen delirium.
The action of benzodiazepines such as lorazepam.
Not the action of haloperidol.
The action of SSRIs.

steps.x: **A. Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors.** Delirium: cholinergic deficiency + dopaminergic excess.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman takes eight regular medicines and has mild memory problems. She develops delirium from a mild urinary infection with a temperature of 37.6°C. Her 45 year old daughter had the same infection last month and stayed completely lucid.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the mother developed delirium?
questions.e: Older patients have reduced cognitive reserve and often polypharmacy, so a minor insult such as a mild UTI can tip them into delirium.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Same **minor** insult, different **brain reserve**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reduced cognitive reserve and polypharmacy.

elim: The infection was mild.
Mild infection with a low temperature.
Delirium is not caused by structural disease.
Both are women.

steps.x: **D. Reduced cognitive reserve and polypharmacy.** Older people: low reserve + polypharmacy, so minor insults cause delirium.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with Parkinson's disease has delirium. A locum gives him IM haloperidol for agitation. The next day he is rigid, cannot get out of bed and his tremor is much worse.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
questions.e: Haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors, worsening the dopamine deficit of Parkinson's disease and causing extrapyramidal effects. That is why lorazepam is used instead.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
A **dopamine antagonist** in a patient who is **dopamine deficient**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dopamine blockade.

elim: Haloperidol is not mainly anticholinergic; this is parkinsonism.
The action of benzodiazepines.
Not caused by a single dose of haloperidol.
Serotonin syndrome is caused by serotonergic drugs.

steps.x: **B. Dopamine receptor blockade.** Antipsychotics are avoided in Parkinson's/Lewy body dementia: extrapyramidal effects.
